{{short description|Geometry; how many 3-point lines can n points form}}
{{distinguish|Euclid's orchard}}
[[File:Orchard-planting problem.svg|thumb|An arrangement of nine points (related to the [[Pappus configuration]]) forming ten 3-point lines.]]

In [[discrete geometry]], the original '''orchard-planting problem''' (or the '''tree-planting problem''') asks for the maximum number of 3-point [[Line (geometry)|lines]] attainable by a [[Configuration (geometry)|configuration]] of a specific number of [[Point (geometry)|points]] in the [[euclidean plane|plane]]. There are also investigations into how many {{mvar|k}}-point lines there can be. [[Hallard T. Croft]] and [[Paul Erdős]] proved
<math display=block>t_k > \frac{cn^2}{k^3},</math> 
where {{mvar|n}} is the number of points and {{mvar|t<sub>k</sub>}} is the number of {{mvar|k}}-point lines.<ref>''The Handbook of Combinatorics'', edited by [[László Lovász]],  [[Ronald Graham (mathematician)|Ron Graham]], et al, in the chapter titled ''Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry'' by [[Paul Erdős]] and [[George B. Purdy]].</ref> 
Their construction contains some {{mvar|m}}-point lines, where {{math|''m'' > ''k''}}. One can also ask the question if these are not allowed.

==Integer sequence==
[[File:orchard_planting_problem.svg|thumb|Maximum possible number of 3-point lines 𝑡<sub>3</sub> for 𝑛 from 3 to 11.<ref>http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Orchard-PlantingProblem.html</ref><ref>http://blog.wolfram.com/2018/02/02/cultivating-new-solutions-for-the-orchard-planting-problem</ref>]]
Define {{tmath|t_3^\text{orchard}(n)}} to be the  maximum number of 3-point lines attainable with a configuration of {{mvar|n}} points. 
For an arbitrary number of {{mvar|n}} points, {{tmath|t_3^\text{orchard}(n)}} was shown to be  <math>\tfrac{1}{6}n^2 - O(n)</math> in 1974.

The first few values of {{tmath|t_3^\text{orchard}(n)}} are given in the following table {{OEIS|A003035}}.

==Upper and lower bounds==
Since no two lines may share two distinct points, a [[Triviality (mathematics)|trivial]] [[Upper and lower bounds|upper-bound]] for the number of 3-point lines determined by {{mvar|n}} points is
<math display=block>\left\lfloor \binom{n}{2} \Big/ \binom{3}{2} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{n^2-n}{6} \right\rfloor.</math>
Using the fact that  [[Sylvester–Gallai theorem#The number of ordinary lines|the number of 2-point lines]] is at least {{tmath|\tfrac{6n}{13} }} {{harv|Csima|Sawyer|1993}}, this upper bound can be lowered to
<math display=block>\left\lfloor \frac{\binom{n}{2} - \frac{6n}{13}}{3} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{n^2}{6} - \frac{25n}{78} \right\rfloor.</math>

Lower bounds for {{tmath|t_3^\text{orchard}(n)}} are given by constructions for sets of points with many 3-point lines. The earliest quadratic lower bound of <math>\approx \tfrac{1}{8}n^2</math> was given by [[James Joseph Sylvester|Sylvester]], who placed {{mvar|n}} points on the cubic curve {{math|1=''y'' = ''x''<sup>3</sup>}}.  This was improved to <math>\tfrac{1}{6}n^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}n + 1</math> in 1974 by {{harvs|author1-link=Stefan Burr|last1=Burr|author2-link=Branko Grünbaum|last2=Grünbaum|author3-link=Neil Sloane|last3=Sloane|year=1974|txt}}, using a construction based on [[Weierstrass's elliptic functions]].  An elementary construction using [[hypocycloid]]s was found by {{harvtxt|Füredi|Palásti|1984}} achieving the same lower bound.

In September 2013, [[Ben Joseph Green|Ben Green]] and [[Terence Tao]] published a paper in which they prove that for all point sets of sufficient size, {{math|''n'' &gt; ''n''<sub>0</sub>}}, there are at most 
<math display=block>\frac{n(n-3)}{6} + 1 =  \frac{1}{6}n^2 - \frac{1}{2}n + 1</math>
3-point lines which matches the lower bound established by Burr, Grünbaum and Sloane.<ref>{{harvtxt|Green|Tao|2013}}</ref> Thus, for sufficiently large {{mvar|n}}, the exact value of {{tmath|t_3^\text{orchard}(n)}} is known.

This is slightly better than the bound that would directly follow from their tight lower bound of {{tmath|\tfrac n 2}} for the number of [[Sylvester–Gallai theorem|2-point lines]]: <math>\tfrac{n(n-2)}{6},</math> proved in the same paper and solving a 1951 problem posed independently by  [[Gabriel Andrew Dirac]] and [[Theodore Motzkin]].

Orchard-planting problem has also been considered over finite fields. In this version of the problem, the {{mvar|n}} points lie in a projective plane defined over a finite field. {{harv|Padmanabhan|Shukla|2020}}.
